correctness.rationale: The unchanged theorem in the replacement RESULT.md is specifically about strict crossings. At the interface the left and right normals are 1−y and a+y. The common-positive interval exists only for a>−1 and the common-negative interval only for a<−1; at a=−1 they never have the same nonzero sign. A periodic trajectory with only strict crossings would require both directions. Neither affine saddle can support a cycle within its own open half-plane. At the benchmark the left coordinates (y−x,y−3x−2) have rates (−1,1), and the right coordinates (x+y−2,y−x+1) have rates (3/2,−1/2). Starting at P+, evaluating at e^(T_L)=(1+δ)/(1−δ)=φ⁶ and e^(T_R/2)=(2+δ)/(2−δ)=φ² gives P− in each case. Strict convexity on the left and strict concavity of x_R(t) on the right give the correct interior signs between the contacts. At P+ the normals are (−δ,δ−1/4), and at P− they are (δ,−δ−1/4), so these are repelling and attracting sliding contacts respectively, not fold points. The Filippov tangential field on y<1 is (6y²−5y−2)/(9−8y). Its denominator is positive and its only root on that component is (5−√73)/12; its sign points toward the root on both sides. Each sliding solution is confined between its initial ordinate and the root, hence is global forward and converges. The slope at the root is −3√73/(17+2√73). value.rationale: This is a checkable counterexample to inferring actual cycling from matched polynomial level sets, tied to a published example claimed to witness sharpness. The strict-crossing obstruction is robust to the two forcing parameters; the exact clocks and sliding capture explain what the two advertised arcs actually do. The correction is valuable even though its decisive interface test is short.
